How to Fix Disconnected & Reversed Arabic Text in Python (ReportLab & Matplotlib Guide)

If you have ever tried generating an automated PDF report or plotting data charts in Python with Arabic text, you know the heartbreak. Before writing custom scripts, you can also test your strings instantly using our browser-based Arabic Text Normalizer Tool.

Instead of clean, connected script, your text outputs as isolated, backward letter blocks. Words spell backward from left to right, and cursive ligatures shatter completely.

This happens because standard Python graphics and PDF engines lack built-in bidirectional (BiDi) parsing and OpenType Arabic shaping tables.

Here is how you fix it for good using arabic_reshaper and python-bidi.

Why Python Breaks Arabic Text Rendering

Standard Python libraries treat Arabic like Latin text by rendering character byte codes sequentially without applying cursive positioning or right-to-left line flows.

When you pass a raw UTF-8 Arabic string into ReportLab or Matplotlib, two major failures happen under the hood.

First, the renderer does not recognize that Arabic is a cursive script. It pulls the isolated form of every single letter from the font file.

Second, it ignores the Right-to-Left (RTL) reading direction. The entire string gets reversed, turning words inside out.

To make matters worse, standard system fonts lack the glyph substitution rules required to bridge characters together. If you need to clean up legacy text strings before processing them in your backend, try our Arabic Text Normalization Utility.

Fixing ReportLab Arabic Paragraphs and Disconnected Letters

To fix disconnected Arabic letters in ReportLab PDFs, you must first reshape the string using arabic_reshaper and then reorder the character array using python-bidi before passing it to a paragraph style with an Arabic-compatible font.

ReportLab builds static PDFs using basic canvas drawing and paragraph flowables. It cannot handle RTL text reordering natively.

You need two helper packages installed in your environment:

pip install arabic_reshaper python-bidi reportlab

Here is the exact code pattern to sanitize and render Arabic strings inside a ReportLab story flowable:

from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet, ParagraphStyle
from reportlab.pdfbase import pdfmetrics
from reportlab.pdfbase.ttfonts import TTFont
import arabic_reshaper
from bidi.algorithm import get_display

# 1. Register a TrueType font that supports Arabic (e.g., Cairo or Amiri)
pdfmetrics.registerFont(TTFont('Cairo', 'Cairo-Regular.ttf'))

# 2. Prepare and fix the raw Arabic text string
raw_text = "تقرير مبيعات النظام المالي"
reshaped_text = arabic_reshaper.reshape(raw_text)
bidi_text = get_display(reshaped_text)

# 3. Setup ReportLab document
doc = SimpleDocTemplate("arabic_report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

arabic_style = ParagraphStyle(
    'ArabicStyle',
    parent=styles['Normal'],
    fontName='Cairo',
    fontSize=14,
    alignment=2 # Right alignment
)

story = [Paragraph(bidi_text, arabic_style)]
doc.build(story)

Fixing Matplotlib Right-to-Left Arabic Text and Labels

To make Matplotlib render Arabic axis labels and titles correctly, you must pass your text through arabic_reshaper and python-bidi while explicitly setting the font properties to a local Unicode typeface.

Matplotlib uses FreeType for text rendering. By default, its layout engine assumes every string flows from left to right.

If you plot a chart with Arabic labels without preprocessing, your graph will show backward floating characters.

Here is how you format your titles and axis ticks in Python:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import arabic_reshaper
from bidi.algorithm import get_display

def fix_arabic(text):
    return get_display(arabic_reshaper.reshape(text))

# Sample data
x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [10, 20, 25, 30]

plt.plot(x, y)

# Apply fixes to chart elements
plt.title(fix_arabic("معدل نمو الأرباح الشهرية"), fontname="Cairo")
plt.xlabel(fix_arabic("الشهر"), fontname="Cairo")
plt.ylabel(fix_arabic("القيمة بالدولار"), fontname="Cairo")

plt.savefig("arabic_chart.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

Handling Complex Data Pipelines and Databases

When pulling Arabic text strings from legacy SQL databases or CSV data pipelines, run a centralized sanitization function before passing data to your PDF or image renderers.

Data pipelines often inject invisible Unicode control characters, extra whitespace, or broken UTF-8 byte sequences.

If your strings pass straight from a database into your reshaping function, you will still encounter rendering errors.

Always normalize your text inputs first:

import re
import arabic_reshaper
from bidi.algorithm import get_display

def clean_and_prepare_arabic(text: str) -> str:
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        return ""
    
    # Strip excessive whitespace and zero-width spaces
    cleaned = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()
    
    # Apply Arabic reshaping and bidirectional reordering
    reshaped = arabic_reshaper.reshape(cleaned)
    return get_display(reshaped)

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Why does my text still look backward after using arabic_reshaper?

You missed the bidirectional reordering step. arabic_reshaper only fixes the character shapes (cursive connections). You must wrap that output inside bidi.algorithm.get_display() from the python-bidi package to flip the word order from right to left.

Can ReportLab render Arabic without external helper libraries?

No. ReportLab's native canvas and paragraph engines do not include an integrated OpenType GPOS shaping engine or BiDi layout processor. External text preprocessing is mandatory.

Which TrueType fonts work best for Python PDF generation?

Always use modern OpenType Unicode fonts that contain complete Arabic glyph tables. Recommended options include Cairo, Tajawal, Amiri, and Readex Pro available via Google Fonts.
